Rule 412(c)'s procedure applies to evidence within Rule 412. A prior false accusation falls outside the rule.
The Confrontation Clause protects cross on bias and similar subjects, but it does not abolish ordinary limits such as 608(b)'s extrinsic-evidence bar.
Correct. False-accusation evidence is credibility evidence outside 412, but it remains subject to 403, the Huddleston threshold, and 608(b)'s bar on extrinsic proof of character for truthfulness.
topic: Impeachment & the rape shield — FRE 412 · FRE 608(b)

q:
In a civil sexual-harassment suit, the defendant employer wants to offer evidence of the plaintiff's sexual conduct with coworkers and of her reputation for promiscuity.

Which statement correctly describes Rule 412 in this case?
o: Rule 412 does not apply, because it governs only criminal prosecutions for sexual assault.
The evidence is admissible if its probative value is not substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice, the ordinary Rule 403 test.
The evidence is admissible only to prove that someone other than the defendant was the source of physical evidence.
The conduct only if its probative value substantially outweighs harm and prejudice; reputation only if she put it in issue.
The evidence is inadmissible in all circumstances, because civil cases have no exceptions to Rule 412.
e: Rule: In a civil case, the court may admit evidence offered to prove a victim's sexual behavior or predisposition if its probative value substantially outweighs the danger of harm to any victim and of unfair prejudice to any party; reputation evidence only if the victim has placed it in controversy (FRE 412(b)(2)).
oe: Rule 412 applies in any "civil or criminal proceeding involving alleged sexual misconduct," including harassment suits.
Rule 412(b)(2) reverses the ordinary balance: probative value must substantially outweigh the dangers.
That is one of the criminal-case exceptions in 412(b)(1). Civil cases use a balancing test.

Correct. That is Rule 412(b)(2)'s reverse balancing test, with its special limit on reputation evidence. The proponent must also follow 412(c): a motion at least 14 days before trial, notice to the victim, and a sealed in camera hearing.
Civil cases have the 412(b)(2) balancing exception.
topic: Impeachment & the rape shield — FRE 412(b)(2) · FRE 412(c)

q: Which impeachment evidence is admissible?
o: In a criminal case, the defendant's juvenile adjudication for theft, offered to impeach him when he testifies.
A prosecution witness's juvenile fraud adjudication in a criminal case, when necessary to determine guilt fairly.
Evidence that a witness belongs to a religion whose teachings, the opponent argues, permit lying to outsiders.
In a civil case, a witness's juvenile adjudication for perjury, because crimen falsi are always admissible.
A conviction for fraud that was pardoned on a finding that the witness was innocent.
e: Rule: Juvenile adjudications are admissible only in a criminal case, only against a witness other than the defendant, only if an adult's conviction for that offense would be admissible, and only if necessary to fairly determine guilt or innocence (FRE 609(d)). Religious beliefs may not be used to attack or support credibility (FRE 610).
oe: Rule 609(d) admits juvenile adjudications only against a witness other than the defendant, and only when necessary to fairly determine guilt or innocence.
Correct. Rule 609(d)'s conditions are all met: a criminal case, a witness other than the defendant, an offense that would be admissible against an adult, and necessity.
Rule 610 bars evidence of a witness's religious beliefs or opinions to attack or support credibility.
Rule 609(d) admits juvenile adjudications only in criminal cases.
Rule 609(c) bars a conviction pardoned or annulled on a finding of innocence.
topic: Impeachment & the rape shield — FRE 609(d) · FRE 610

q: Which statement about competency and personal knowledge is correct?
o: A child under ten is incompetent to testify under Rule 601 unless she passes a competency examination.
A hearsay declarant must have had personal knowledge, even under a Rule 803 exception.
An expert witness must have personal knowledge of the facts underlying her opinion.
A witness's own testimony can never establish her personal knowledge; independent evidence is required.
In a federal diversity case, federal law always governs a witness's competency.
e: Rule: Every person is competent to be a witness unless the rules provide otherwise; in civil cases state law governs competency on state-law claims (FRE 601). A witness may testify only on personal knowledge, which the witness's own testimony may establish; this does not apply to experts under 703 (FRE 602).
oe: Rule 601 makes every person competent unless the rules provide otherwise. Federal law presumes children competent and requires compelling reasons for an examination (18 U.S.C. § 3509(c)).
Correct. The ACN to Rule 803 says the declarant must have had firsthand knowledge; neither 803 nor 804 dispenses with it. (Party admissions under 801(d)(2) are the exception: Mahlandt.)
Rule 602 "does not apply to a witness's expert testimony under Rule 703." Experts may rely on facts made known to them.
Rule 602 says the evidence to prove personal knowledge "may consist of the witness's own testimony."
Rule 601's second sentence: in a civil case, state law governs competency regarding a claim or defense for which state law supplies the rule of decision.
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 601 · FRE 602 · FRE 803

q: Which item, offered to prove the fact indicated, is hearsay?
o: A government official's announcement to reporters that he will take his family to a test site, offered to prove the site is safe.
A sea captain's conduct in inspecting his ship and then sailing with his family aboard, offered to prove the ship was seaworthy.
A sailor's failure to pack his bags, offered to prove he did not know he was being transferred.
A caller's words to an apartment's phone, "Put two hundred on the Eagles," offered to prove the apartment was a betting operation.
A car's factory-applied Mercedes star, offered to prove the car was a Mercedes.
e: Rule: A "statement" is a person's oral or written assertion, or nonverbal conduct intended as an assertion (FRE 801(a)). Hearsay is a statement not made while testifying at the current trial, offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted (FRE 801(c)).
oe: Correct. Unlike the captain, the official intended to communicate his belief to an audience. That is an assertion, offered for its truth, and so hearsay.
The captain did not intend to assert anything by sailing. Nonassertive conduct is not a "statement" under 801(a).
This is nonassertive conduct (the Few Good Men example). It depends on his belief, but he did not intend to communicate it.
The callers did not intend to assert that the apartment was a betting shop. Under the FRE, words not intended to assert the fact they are offered to prove are generally not hearsay.
A machine-applied label is not a person's statement. (A fake badge affixed as a disguise could be an intended assertion.)
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(a) · FRE 801(c)

q: Which out-of-court statement is hearsay when offered for the purpose stated?
o: "Watch out for Joey, he carries a gun," told to the defendant, offered to show the defendant reasonably feared Joey.
"I accept your offer of $5,000 for the car," offered to prove a contract was formed.
"I spent all morning with an architect planning my retirement home," offered to prove the speaker was not suicidal.
A testator's chatty letters about family events, offered to prove the testator was mentally competent.
"Does Sarah sell drugs? How else could she afford that car?", offered only to show that the speaker had heard rumors about Sarah.
e: Rule: Whether words are hearsay depends on the proponent's purpose. Words offered for their effect on a listener, as verbal acts, or to prove something disconnected from their contents are not offered for the truth of the matter asserted.
oe: Offered for its effect on the listener, the statement matters whether or not it is true.
Words of acceptance are a verbal act with legal effect, not an assertion offered for its truth.

Correct. The inference runs through the truth of the assertion (he really was planning for the long term), so the statement is hearsay even though the ultimate fact (not suicidal) is not what he asserted.
The letters are offered to prove a fact disconnected from their contents (coherent thought), not the truth of what they say.
Offered only to show the speaker had heard rumors, the words are not offered for their truth. (Offered to prove Sarah sells drugs, the implied assertion would be hearsay.)
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(c)

q:
A robbery victim testifies at trial. The prosecutor asks her what she said when police showed her the defendant in a lineup two days after the robbery, and she answers, "I said, 'That's the robber!'"

Which statement is correct?
o: Her answer is not hearsay, because she is the declarant and is now testifying under oath.
It is an out-of-court statement, but Rule 801(d)(1)(C) excludes it from hearsay.
Her lineup statement is admissible only if she is now unable to identify the defendant in court.
Her lineup statement is inadmissible unless it was made under penalty of perjury.
Her lineup statement is admissible only to rehabilitate her after an attack on her credibility.
e: Rule: A statement is not hearsay if the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination about it, and it identifies a person as someone the declarant perceived earlier (FRE 801(d)(1)(C)).
oe: A witness repeating her own earlier words is still repeating an out-of-court statement. Being on the stand does not change that.

Correct. The statement is hearsay by definition, but Rule 801(d)(1)(C) excludes a prior identification of a person the declarant perceived earlier, when the declarant testifies and is subject to cross about it.
Rule 801(d)(1)(C) does not require that the in-court identification fail or match. Owens admitted a prior identification despite memory loss.
Only prior inconsistent statements ever needed an oath, under 801(d)(1)(A), and the December 1, 2026 amendment removes that requirement too.
That describes prior consistent statements under 801(d)(1)(B). Identifications under (C) are substantive evidence whether or not her credibility was attacked.
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(c) · FRE 801(d)(1)

q:
A wildlife center's education director, who did not see the incident, leaves a note for the center's president: "Sophie bit a child that came in our back yard." Later, the center's board meeting minutes discuss "the legal aspects of the incident of Sophie biting the child." The child sues both the director and the center.

Which statement correctly applies Mahlandt?
o: The note is admissible against both defendants, but the minutes are admissible only against the center.
The note is inadmissible against anyone, because the director had no personal knowledge of the bite.
The note is inadmissible against the center, because a statement to a fellow employee inside the organization is not made to an outsider.
The minutes are admissible against both defendants, because the director worked for the center.
The note and the minutes are admissible against both only if they were against interest when made.
e: Rule: A statement offered against an opposing party is not hearsay if made by the party, adopted by it, made by an authorized spokesperson, made by its agent or employee on a matter within the scope of the relationship while it existed, or made by a coconspirator during and in furtherance of the conspiracy (FRE 801(d)(2)).
oe: Correct. The note is the director's own statement under (A) and the center's agent's statement under (D). The minutes are the center's own statement, not attributable to the director.
Mahlandt held that 801(d)(2) does not require personal knowledge. The trial court's exclusion on that ground was reversed.
Intra-organization statements count. The note was admissible against the center as an agent's statement under (D).
Admissibility is party-specific. The minutes were the center's statement, and the director was not shown to have adopted them.
Party statements need not be against interest when made. That requirement belongs to Rule 804(b)(3).
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(d)(2)(A) · Mahlandt v. Wild Canid Survival & Research Center, Inc.

q:
A trucking company fires a driver the morning after a crash. That afternoon, the driver tells a reporter, "It was on me. I was texting dispatch and never saw the light change." The injured motorist sues the company and the driver together.

How may the driver's statement be used?
o: Against the driver only, because he was fired before he spoke.
Against both defendants, because the statement concerned driving, a matter within the scope of the driver's job.
Against neither, because the driver lacked authority to speak for the company to the press.
Against both, as a statement against interest, because it exposed the driver to civil liability.
Against the driver only if he had personal knowledge of when the light changed.
e: Rule: A statement is not hearsay if offered against a party and made by the party's agent or employee on a matter within the scope of that relationship and while it existed (FRE 801(d)(2)(D)). The statement must be considered but does not by itself establish the relationship.
oe: Correct. The statement is admissible against the driver under 801(d)(2)(A), but under (D) the employment had ended, so it cannot be attributed to the company. The company is entitled to a limiting instruction.
The scope element is met, but Rule 801(d)(2)(D) also requires that the statement be made while the employment relationship existed.
Authority to speak is required under (C), not (D). Under (D), any employee speaking within the scope of the relationship counts. The problem here is timing.
Rule 804(b)(3) requires unavailability, and the driver is in the courtroom.
Party statements need no personal knowledge, and he knew what mattered most: that he was texting.
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(d)(2)(D)

q: In which situation is the defendant's silence most likely admissible as an adoptive admission?
o: At a party, the defendant hears a friend accuse him of stealing a car and laughs without denying it.
After his arrest and Miranda warnings, an officer tells him, "Your partner says you planned the robbery," and he says nothing.
While handcuffed in a squad car before any warnings, he says nothing when an officer remarks that he matches the robber's description.
During a recorded jail visit, after seeing a sign warning that visits are monitored, he says nothing when his daughter accuses him.
In a room so noisy that he may not have heard the accusation, he continues talking with someone else.
e: Rule: A statement is not hearsay if offered against a party who manifested that it adopted it or believed it to be true (FRE 801(d)(2)(B)). Silence is an adoption only if the party heard and understood, was at liberty to respond, the circumstances naturally called for a denial, and the party did not deny it.
oe: Correct. He heard and understood, was free to respond, the accusation naturally called for a denial, and he did not deny it. Non-custodial silence carries no Fifth Amendment protection without express invocation (Salinas).
Using post-Miranda silence would violate due process (Doyle v. Ohio; Wainwright v. Greenfield), because the warnings implicitly promise that silence carries no penalty.
Custodial pre-Miranda silence splits the circuits for substantive use, and an officer's remark may not naturally call for a response.
A person who knows he is being recorded has reason to stay silent, so the silence is ambiguous (Problem 7.14); the habeas courts found its use unconstitutional.
If he did not hear and understand the statement, the first precondition fails.
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(d)(2)(B)

q:
The government offers a recorded statement by one drug dealer to an informant: "My gentleman friend will buy half the kilo." It argues the "friend" was the defendant and that the statement is a coconspirator statement.

Which statement correctly describes the foundation?
o: The jury decides, under Rule 104(b), whether a reasonable jury could find a conspiracy.
The judge finds the foundation by a preponderance and may consider the statement itself, plus other evidence.
The judge must find the conspiracy beyond a reasonable doubt, using only evidence independent of the statement.
The statement is admissible only if the defendant has been charged with conspiracy.
The statement is admissible if made at any time, including after arrest, so long as it describes the conspiracy.
e: Rule: A statement is not hearsay if offered against a party and made by the party's coconspirator during and in furtherance of the conspiracy (FRE 801(d)(2)(E)). The court decides the foundation under 104(a) by a preponderance; the statement must be considered but does not by itself establish the conspiracy or participation.
oe: Bourjaily held that the foundation is a 104(a) question for the judge, not conditional relevance.
Correct. Bourjaily allowed "bootstrapping" under 104(a), and the 1997 amendment adds that the statement alone does not establish the conspiracy or participation.
The standard is a preponderance, and the judge may consider the statement itself.
No conspiracy charge is required; it is enough that the declarant and party were joint venturers, and the venture need not be criminal.
Statements after the conspiracy ends, such as confessions to police, are not "during and in furtherance."
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(d)(2)(E) · Bourjaily v. United States

q:
A witness told police at the station, in a signed and sworn written statement, that she saw the defendant cut and package heroin. She gave the same account to a grand jury. At trial in October 2026, before the December 1, 2026 amendment to Rule 801(d)(1)(A) takes effect, she testifies that she saw nothing and claims not to remember the events.

Which prior statement may be used as substantive evidence?
o: Both, because each was sworn and is inconsistent with her trial testimony.
The grand jury testimony, because it was sworn and given at a proceeding.
Neither, because claimed memory loss is not "inconsistent" with a prior statement.
The stationhouse statement, because it is a written record made when the events were fresh.
Neither, because a witness who claims memory loss is not "subject to cross-examination."
e: Rule: A declarant-witness's prior statement is not hearsay if it is inconsistent with the declarant's testimony and was given under penalty of perjury at a trial, hearing, or other proceeding, or in a deposition (FRE 801(d)(1)(A)).
oe: A stationhouse statement is not given "at a trial, hearing, or other proceeding or in a deposition," even if sworn.

Correct. Rule 801(d)(1)(A) requires the declarant to testify and be subject to cross, an inconsistent statement, an oath, and a proceeding. Grand jury testimony qualifies; the jury may even convict on it.
Many courts treat claimed memory loss as inconsistent, especially when the judge finds it feigned under 104(a).
That describes recorded recollection under 803(5), which also requires the witness to vouch for the record's accuracy. Under 801(d)(1)(A) the stationhouse statement fails the proceeding requirement.
Owens held that a witness who takes the stand and answers questions is subject to cross-examination despite memory loss.
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(d)(1)(A)

q:
A witness texted a friend, not under oath, that she saw the defendant cut and package heroin. In a case filed in 2027, she testifies at trial that she saw nothing, and she is subject to cross-examination about the text.

Under Rule 801(d)(1)(A) as amended effective December 1, 2026, which statement is correct?
o: The text is substantive evidence, because it is inconsistent with her testimony.
The text may only impeach her, because it was not given under oath in a proceeding.
The text is substantive evidence only if it also fits a Rule 803 exception.
The text may be used only with a limiting instruction on its proper use.
The text must be enough by itself to support a conviction, or it is excluded.
e: Rule: As amended effective December 1, 2026, a prior statement is not hearsay if the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination about it and it is inconsistent with the declarant's testimony (FRE 801(d)(1)(A)).
oe: Correct. The amended rule needs only a testifying declarant, cross-examination about the statement, and inconsistency.
That is the rule before December 1, 2026. The amendment deletes the oath-and-proceeding requirement.
A statement that meets Rule 801(d) is not hearsay at all, so it needs no exception.
The Committee Note says a major advantage of the amendment is that it avoids that confusing instruction.
The Committee Note says the rule governs admissibility, not sufficiency.
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(d)(1)(A) (2026 amendment)

q:
A father accused of sexually abusing his daughter argues that the mother concocted the allegations to win custody after she obtained summer visitation. The prosecution offers the daughter's out-of-court statements describing the abuse, all made after the summer visitation began.

Which statement reflects Tome and the current rule?
o: Not under (B)(i), because they postdate the alleged motive, though (B)(ii) may admit them to rebut other attacks.
The statements are admissible under 801(d)(1)(B)(i), because any consistent statement rebuts a charge of fabrication.
The statements are admissible, because the timing of a consistent statement goes only to its weight.
The statements are inadmissible, because consistent statements may never be used as substantive evidence.
The statements are admissible only if the child is unavailable at trial.
e: Rule: A prior consistent statement is not hearsay if the declarant testifies, is subject to cross, and the statement is offered (i) to rebut a charge of recent fabrication or improper influence or motive, or (ii) to rehabilitate the declarant's credibility when attacked on another ground (FRE 801(d)(1)(B)).
oe: Correct. Tome codified the common-law pre-motive requirement. The 2014 amendment adds (B)(ii) for attacks on other grounds, such as inconsistency or faulty memory, but Tome still governs (B)(i).
Tome held that a consistent statement rebuts a charge of recent fabrication or improper motive only if made before the alleged motive arose.
That was the Tome dissent's view (Breyer, J.). The majority rejected it.
Statements meeting 801(d)(1)(B) are substantive evidence, not merely rehabilitation.
Rule 801(d)(1) requires the declarant to testify and be subject to cross-examination.
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(d)(1)(B) · Tome v. United States

q:
A prison counselor beaten with a pipe identified the defendant from a photo array weeks after the attack. At trial, he remembers making the identification but, because of his head injuries, cannot remember seeing his attacker.

Under Owens, is the prior identification admissible?
o: No, because a witness who cannot recall the basis of his identification is not "subject to cross-examination."
No, because the Confrontation Clause guarantees cross-examination that is effective in exposing the basis of the identification.
Yes, but only if the prosecution first shows the identification was made under oath.
Yes, because the witness testified and answered questions, and the defense could expose his memory loss to the jury.
Yes, because a victim's statements identifying his attacker are dying declarations.
e: Rule: A witness's prior identification of a person is not hearsay if the witness testifies and is subject to cross-examination about it (FRE 801(d)(1)(C)). Memory loss does not make the witness unavailable for cross-examination under the rule or the Confrontation Clause (Owens).
oe: Owens held that a witness who testifies and answers questions is subject to cross-examination, despite memory loss.
The Clause guarantees "an opportunity for effective cross-examination, not cross-examination that is effective in whatever way, and to whatever extent, the defense might wish."
No oath is required for identifications under (C).
Correct. Rule 801(d)(1)(C) and the Confrontation Clause are satisfied by the opportunity for cross, and the defense can use the memory loss to undermine the identification.
The counselor did not die or believe death was imminent, and the identification comes in under (C).
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 801(d)(1)(C) · United States v. Owens

q:
A prosecution witness testifies that the defendant admitted taking part in a theft. The defense calls two people who heard the witness say, a month later, that he knew the defendant was not involved. The defense never asked the witness about that remark on cross-examination. Trial is in October 2026, before the December 1, 2026 amendment to Rule 801(d)(1)(A) takes effect.

Which statement is correct?
o: The remarks are admissible as substantive evidence that the defendant was not involved.
The remarks are inadmissible for any purpose, because they are hearsay with no exception.
The remarks are admissible only if the defense first showed the witness a written copy of them.
They impeach only, and since 2024 the witness must first get a chance to explain or deny them.
The remarks are barred by Rule 608(b) as extrinsic evidence of a witness's untruthfulness.
e: Rule: Unless the court orders otherwise, extrinsic evidence of a witness's prior inconsistent statement may not be admitted until after the witness is given an opportunity to explain or deny it and an adverse party may examine the witness about it. This does not apply to an opposing party's statement (FRE 613(b), as amended 2024).
oe: The remarks were not made under penalty of perjury at a proceeding, so they cannot come in under 801(d)(1)(A). They impeach only.
Offered only to show that the witness said something inconsistent, they are not offered for their truth.
Rule 613(a) does not require showing the statement to the witness, only disclosing it to opposing counsel on request.
Correct. Barrett allowed the opportunity to come at any time, but since Dec. 1, 2024, Rule 613(b) requires the foundation first, unless the court orders otherwise.
Prior inconsistent statements impeach by inconsistency, not by character, so 608(b) does not apply; 613 governs.
topic: Competency, hearsay definition & 801(d) — FRE 613(b) · United States v. Barrett

q: In which situation is the declarant "unavailable" under Rule 804(a)?
o: The declarant is in the courtroom and willing to testify, but the proponent prefers to use her earlier statement.
The declarant fled because the proponent threatened her to keep her from testifying.
The declarant lives out of state, and the proponent did not try to subpoena her or arrange her deposition.
She takes the stand and validly invokes the Fifth Amendment about the subject of her statement.
The declarant is available but would testify inconsistently with her statement.
e: Rule: A declarant is unavailable if exempted by a privilege ruling, refusing to testify despite an order, testifying to not remembering the subject matter, dead or ill, or absent and not procurable by process or other reasonable means. Unavailability procured by the proponent to prevent testimony does not count (FRE 804(a)).
oe: A present, willing declarant is available. Rule 804 exceptions are not a way to avoid calling her.
Rule 804(a) does not apply if the proponent procured or wrongfully caused the unavailability to prevent testimony.
Rule 804(a)(5) requires that the proponent could not procure her attendance (and, for some exceptions, her testimony) by process or other reasonable means.
Correct. Unavailability concerns the declarant's testimony, not her physical presence. A declarant exempted by a privilege ruling is unavailable under 804(a)(1).
Expected inconsistency is not unavailability. The proponent can call her and use 801(d)(1)(A) or 613.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 804(a)

q:
A man acquitted of battering two police officers sues them for excessive force and then dies. His estate offers his testimony from the criminal trial, where he was cross-examined by the state prosecutor. The officers object that they were not parties to the criminal case.

How did the court in Volland-Golden rule?
o: Exclude the testimony, because the party against whom former testimony is offered must have had the opportunity to cross-examine.
Exclude the testimony, because a criminal trial and a civil suit can never involve a similar motive.
Admit the testimony under Rule 804(b)(2), because the declarant is dead.
Admit it, because the State had a similar motive to discredit him and so was the officers' predecessor in interest.
Admit the testimony only if the officers testified at the criminal trial and were cross-examined there.
e: Rule: Former testimony is admissible if the declarant is unavailable and the testimony is offered against a party who had, or in a civil case whose predecessor in interest had, an opportunity and similar motive to develop it by direct, cross, or redirect examination (FRE 804(b)(1)).
oe: That is the rule in criminal cases. In civil cases, a "predecessor in interest" with an opportunity and similar motive suffices.
Volland-Golden found a similar motive: both trials turned on the same sequence of events and the reasonableness of force.
Death establishes unavailability, not an exception. Dying declarations require a belief that death was imminent.
Correct. The court read "predecessor in interest" by its common meaning plus a similar stake, and applied the Feldman factors: type of proceeding, strategy, stakes, and issues.
The question is whether the party against whom the testimony is offered (or a predecessor) had the opportunity to examine the declarant, not whether the officers were examined.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 804(b)(1) · Volland-Golden v. City of Chicago

q:
A woman who later died said to her nurse, "Dr. Shepard has poisoned me." Her doctors had told her she was improving, and she lived almost a month afterward.

Why was her statement inadmissible as a dying declaration?
o: Because she lacked a settled, hopeless expectation that death was near.
Because she was not the defendant's wife at the time of the statement.
Because dying declarations are admissible only in civil cases.
Because a dying declaration must be made within hours of death.
Because the declarant must actually die for the exception to apply.
e: Rule: In a prosecution for homicide or in a civil case, a statement that the declarant made, while believing the declarant's death to be imminent, about its cause or circumstances (FRE 804(b)(2)).
oe: Correct. Cardozo required that the declarant speak "without hope of recovery and in the shadow of impending death," shown by the evidence and not left to conjecture.
Marriage is irrelevant to dying declarations.
Rule 804(b)(2) applies in homicide prosecutions and civil cases.
The rule has no fixed time limit; what matters is the declarant's belief when she spoke.
Under Rule 804(b)(2), the declarant need only be unavailable. Here she did die, but the belief requirement failed.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 804(b)(2) · Shepard v. United States

q:
After police find cocaine in the trunk of the car he is driving, an arrested courier tells an agent: "I knew the cocaine was in the trunk. It belongs to Williamson, who was driving ahead of me." The courier refuses to testify at Williamson's trial.

How should the court apply Rule 804(b)(3)?
o: Admit the whole confession, because it was against the courier's penal interest as a whole.
Exclude the whole confession, because statements to police can never be against the declarant's interest.
Admit the parts naming Williamson, because collateral statements in a self-inculpatory narrative carry the same reliability.
Exclude the confession, because the courier is not unavailable.
Admit only his self-inculpatory statements, such as knowing of the cocaine, and exclude those blaming Williamson.
e: Rule: A statement against interest is one that a reasonable person in the declarant's position would have made only if believing it true because it was so contrary to the declarant's pecuniary or proprietary interest or so exposed him to civil or criminal liability; in a criminal case it must be supported by corroborating circumstances clearly indicating trustworthiness (FRE 804(b)(3)).
oe: Williamson rejected treating a narrative as a unit. Each declaration must itself be self-inculpatory.
Statements to police can be against interest, as the courier's admission of knowledge was. The problem is parsing.
That was the view of Justice Kennedy's concurrence in the judgment. The majority required each statement to be self-inculpatory.
A declarant who refuses to testify despite a court order, or validly invokes a privilege, is unavailable under 804(a).

Correct. The court must parse the confession. The courier's knowledge was against his interest; the statements implicating Williamson were not, and arrest statements of a codefendant are viewed "with special suspicion."
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 804(b)(3) · Williamson v. United States

q: Which statement about Rule 804(b)(3) is correct?
o: The test is subjective: the proponent must show the declarant actually understood that the statement hurt his interests.
A statement exposing the declarant to social disgrace, such as confessing an affair, qualifies as against interest.
Corroboration may be supplied by the defendant's own testimony that the declarant committed the crime.
In a criminal case, penal-interest statements need clear corroboration whichever side offers them.
A statement against interest is admissible whether or not the declarant is available.
e: Rule: Rule 804(b)(3) uses an objective test, lists pecuniary, proprietary, claim-invalidating, and liability interests, and in criminal cases requires corroborating circumstances that clearly indicate trustworthiness, considering the totality of circumstances and any evidence that supports or undermines the statement.
oe: The test is objective: whether a reasonable person in the declarant's position would have made the statement only if true.
Congress deleted the Supreme Court's proposed "hatred, ridicule, or disgrace" category. Social disgrace is not a listed interest.
The House Judiciary Committee demanded "clear" corroboration precisely because the accused's testimony could otherwise suffice.

Correct. Since 2010 the corroboration requirement applies to penal-interest statements offered by either the prosecution or the defense, and the 2024 amendment adds a totality-of-circumstances inquiry.
Rule 804(b)(3) requires unavailability. That is why Chambers could not have used it: the declarant was in the courtroom.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 804(b)(3)

q:
A defendant kills her husband a week before he is to testify against her in an assault trial. Years later, she is prosecuted for insurance fraud arising from his death, and the government offers his earlier statements to relatives describing her threats.

Which statement correctly applies Rule 804(b)(6)?
o: The statements are inadmissible, because forfeiture applies only at the trial the declarant was supposed to testify in.
The statements are admissible against her merely because she killed him, whatever her purpose.
They are admissible if the court finds she killed him intending to prevent his testimony, in any later proceeding.
The statements are admissible only if her wrongdoing was a crime of which she was convicted.
The statements are admissible only if the jury finds beyond a reasonable doubt that she killed him to stop his testimony.
e: Rule: A statement is not excluded by the hearsay rule if offered against a party that wrongfully caused, or acquiesced in wrongfully causing, the declarant's unavailability as a witness, and did so intending that result (FRE 804(b)(6)).
oe: The Fourth Circuit rejected that limit in the Week 7 reading on these facts: the rule requires only that the defendant intentionally caused the unavailability "as a witness."
Giles and the rule require intent to make the declarant unavailable as a witness. Murder alone is not enough unless preventing testimony was a purpose.
Correct. Forfeiture extends to any later proceeding. The intent requirement is about silencing a witness, not about the particular case, and the court decides it under 104(a).
Wrongdoing need not be criminal or result in a conviction, and acquiescence counts.
The court, not the jury, decides the foundation under 104(a), by a preponderance.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 804(b)(6) · Giles v. California

q:
A coconspirator's statement implicating the defendant is admitted against him under Rule 801(d)(2)(E). The coconspirator does not testify. The defense wants to impeach him with (1) a statement he made to a friend saying the defendant had nothing to do with the scheme, and (2) his prior fraud conviction.

Which statement is correct?
o: Both are admissible to impeach him as if he had testified, without the Rule 613(b) foundation.
Neither is admissible, because the coconspirator never testified and so cannot be impeached.
The inconsistent statement is inadmissible, because the coconspirator never had a chance to explain or deny it.
Only the conviction is admissible, because Rule 806 incorporates Rule 609 but not Rule 613.
Both are admissible as substantive evidence that the defendant is innocent.
e: Rule: When a hearsay statement, or a statement under Rule 801(d)(2)(C), (D), or (E), has been admitted, the declarant's credibility may be attacked, and then supported, by any evidence that would be admissible if the declarant had testified (FRE 806).
oe: Correct. Rule 806 lets the opponent use inconsistent statements, convictions under 609, and character evidence under 608 against an absent declarant.
Rule 806 expressly allows attacking the credibility of a hearsay declarant, including a coconspirator under 801(d)(2)(E).
Rule 806 provides that the court may admit the declarant's inconsistent statement "regardless of when it occurred or whether the declarant had an opportunity to explain or deny it."
Rule 806 covers inconsistent statements directly, without the 613(b) foundation.
Under Rule 806 they impeach the declarant's credibility. Substantive use would need a hearsay exception.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 806

q:
A motorist calls 911 and, in a calm and even voice, says, "A red pickup just passed me doing about a hundred, weaving across all three lanes." The call is offered in a wrongful-death suit to prove the pickup was speeding.

Which statement is correct?
o: The call fails as a present sense impression, because the caller was not under the stress of excitement.
It qualifies as a present sense impression; the calm tone matters only to an excited-utterance theory.
The call qualifies as an excited utterance, because any 911 call concerns a startling event.
The call is admissible only if the caller is unavailable.
The call is inadmissible, because a caller's personal knowledge cannot be shown without identifying him.
e: Rule: A present sense impression is a statement describing or explaining an event or condition, made while or immediately after the declarant perceived it (FRE 803(1)). An excited utterance is a statement relating to a startling event, made while the declarant was under the stress of excitement it caused (FRE 803(2)).
oe: Rule 803(1) has no excitement requirement. Its reliability comes from contemporaneity.
Correct. "Just passed me" shows near-contemporaneity. A calm voice would hurt an argument under 803(2), whose stress requirement is subjective.
The declarant must be under the stress of excitement; a calm caller cuts against 803(2).
Rule 803 exceptions apply regardless of availability.
Personal knowledge can be inferred from the content and circumstances of the statement.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 803(1) · FRE 803(2)

q:
A man writes to his fiancée, "I am leaving Wichita next week with a Mr. Hillmon, a sheep trader." The letter is offered to prove that the writer went west and that he went with Hillmon.

Which statement best describes the use of the letter today?
o: It is inadmissible, because statements of future intent are statements of belief barred by Rule 803(3).
It can prove his intent and that he went, but using it to prove Hillmon went with him is contested.
It is admissible to prove both men's conduct, because the House report endorsed Hillmon in full.
It is admissible only if the writer is unavailable.
It is inadmissible, because the letter was written before any controversy arose.
e: Rule: A statement of the declarant's then-existing state of mind (such as motive, intent, or plan) is not excluded by the hearsay rule, but a statement of memory or belief to prove the fact remembered or believed is, unless it relates to the declarant's will (FRE 803(3)).
oe: Forward-looking intent is a then-existing state of mind. Rule 803(3) admits it, and it may be used to prove the declarant later acted on it.

Correct. Hillmon admitted the letters. But the inference to Hillmon's conduct depends on a statement of memory about another person's intent, which 803(3) does not cover, and the circuits split, some requiring independent corroboration (Pheaster).
The House Judiciary Committee report said 803(3) should limit Hillmon so a declarant's statement of intent is not admissible to prove another person's conduct.
Rule 803 exceptions apply whether or not the declarant is available.
Writing before any controversy is reassuring, not disqualifying.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 803(3) · Mutual Life Insurance Co. v. Hillmon

q:
An assault victim tells an emergency-room nurse that she was "kicked in the head by my baby's father." The prosecution offers the statement under Rule 803(4), but no witness testifies about how the attacker's identity mattered to her treatment.

Which statement best describes the analysis?
o: The entire statement is admissible, because everything a patient tells a nurse is reasonably pertinent to treatment.
The statement is inadmissible, because Rule 803(4) covers only statements made to physicians.
"Kicked in the head" comes in, but identity needs a foundation showing it mattered to treatment.
The identity is always admissible in domestic-violence cases, because safety planning is part of treatment.
The statement is admissible only if made for treatment, not if made to a doctor consulted only for diagnosis.
e: Rule: A statement made for, and reasonably pertinent to, medical diagnosis or treatment, describing medical history, past or present symptoms, their inception, or their general cause, is not excluded by the hearsay rule (FRE 803(4)).
oe: Statements of fault and the assailant's identity are ordinarily not pertinent to diagnosis or treatment.
Rule 803(4) covers statements to anyone involved in care, including nurses.

Correct. The Iowa Supreme Court in State v. Smith held that identity may be pertinent in domestic-violence cases, as with child abuse, but the State must show why with foundation testimony. It reversed for lack of that showing.
That was the dissent's proposed categorical rule. The majority required a case-specific showing.
Rule 803(4) covers statements "made for — and reasonably pertinent to — medical diagnosis or treatment," including diagnosis for litigation.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 803(4) · State v. Smith

q:
A witness who told a detective on the night of a shooting that "Little Arnold" was the shooter takes the stand and says he does not remember giving the statement, what he said, or what happened. The prosecution reads his statement to the jury as a recorded recollection.

Why was this error in Johnson v. State?
o: Because a recorded recollection must be made by the witness himself, not by a detective.
Because the statement was not made at or near the time of the events.
Because the witness never vouched that the statement accurately reflected his knowledge when made.
Because recorded recollection may be received as an exhibit only, never read to the jury.
Because a witness who forgets must first be shown the statement to refresh his memory under Rule 612.
e: Rule: A record is admissible if it is on a matter the witness once knew but now cannot recall well enough to testify fully and accurately, was made or adopted when the matter was fresh, and accurately reflects the witness's knowledge; it may be read in but received as an exhibit only if offered by an adverse party (FRE 803(5)).
oe: Rule 803(5) covers a record "made or adopted by the witness," so a detective's record the witness adopted could qualify.
The statement was made that night, so it was fresh.
Correct. The fourth element of past recollection recorded is that the witness vouches for the record's accuracy. A hostile witness who disowns the statement cannot supply that foundation.
Backwards. The record may be read into evidence but received as an exhibit only if offered by an adverse party.
Refreshing is an option, not a prerequisite. The fatal defect was the missing vouching element.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 612 · FRE 803(5) · Johnson v. State

q: Which record is most likely admissible for its truth under Rule 803(6)?
o: A nurse's contemporaneous chart entry of the patient's vital signs, made in the regular course of care.
A railroad's statement from its engineer, taken by a company official two days after a crossing accident, describing the warning signals.
A police report recording a bystander's account of how an accident happened.
A store's report of a customer's complaint, offered to prove the customer's description of the defect.
A record whose opponent shows the source of information indicates a lack of trustworthiness.
e: Rule: A record of an act, event, condition, opinion, or diagnosis is admissible if made at or near the time by, or from information transmitted by, someone with knowledge, kept in the course of a regularly conducted activity as a regular practice, shown by a custodian, qualified witness, or certification, and the opponent does not show a lack of trustworthiness (FRE 803(6)).
oe: Correct. The record was made at or near the time by someone with knowledge, in the course of a regularly conducted activity, as a regular practice.
Palmer v. Hoffman excluded such a report: a railroad's business is railroading, not litigating, and the report was "calculated for use essentially in the court."
The bystander had no business duty to report. Under Johnson v. Lutz, a stranger's statement in a business record needs its own exception (805).
The customer is an outsider with no business duty, so the description is a second hearsay layer (it might come in for notice).
Rule 803(6)(E) excludes the record if the opponent shows untrustworthiness, and since 2014 the opponent bears that burden.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 803(6) · Palmer v. Hoffman · Johnson v. Lutz

q: In a criminal prosecution, which use of a public record is permitted by Rule 803(8)?
o: The defendant offers factual findings from a legally authorized government investigation that support his defense.
The prosecution offers a police officer's report of what he observed at the crime scene.
The prosecution offers factual findings from an agency investigation concluding the defendant committed fraud.
The prosecution relabels a police report as a business record under Rule 803(6) to avoid 803(8)'s limits.
The prosecution proves the absence of a public record by a certificate without giving any notice to the defendant.
e: Rule: A public office's record of its activities, of matters observed under a legal duty (excluding, in criminal cases, matters observed by law enforcement), or, in civil cases or against the government in criminal cases, factual findings from a legally authorized investigation, is admissible unless the opponent shows a lack of trustworthiness (FRE 803(8)).
oe: Correct. Rule 803(8)(A)(iii) admits factual findings "in a civil case or against the government in a criminal case."
Rule 803(8)(A)(ii) excludes, in a criminal case, matters observed by law-enforcement personnel.
Investigative findings under (A)(iii) are admissible only in civil cases or against the government in criminal cases.
Courts generally do not let prosecutors evade 803(8)'s criminal-case limits this way (United States v. Oates).
Rule 803(10) requires the prosecutor in a criminal case to give written notice at least 14 days before trial, and the defendant may object within 7 days.
topic: 803–806 exceptions — FRE 803(8) · FRE 803(10)

q: Which statement about the residual exception, as amended in 2019, is correct?
o: The statement must have circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness "equivalent" to those of the Rule 803 and 804 exceptions.
A statement that nearly satisfies an enumerated exception, such as a business record without a qualified witness, can never be admitted under Rule 807.
It must have sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness and be more probative than other reasonably obtainable evidence.
Notice may be given orally at any time before the statement is offered.
The proponent must also show that admitting the statement serves the interests of justice and concerns a material fact.
e: Rule: A hearsay statement not admissible under Rule 803 or 804 is not excluded if it is supported by sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness, considering the totality of circumstances and any corroboration, and is more probative on the point than any other evidence the proponent can reasonably obtain, with written pretrial notice of its substance and the declarant's name (FRE 807).
oe: The 2019 amendment dropped the "equivalent" requirement in favor of "sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness."
The amendment's "not admissible under a hearsay exception in Rule 803 or 804" ends the near-miss debate: near misses may be considered (as in Laster).
Correct. Those are the two requirements of 807(a), plus the notice requirement of 807(b).

Notice must be in writing before trial, including the statement's substance and the declarant's name, unless the court excuses it for good cause, in which case it may be given in any form during trial.
The 2019 amendment deleted those requirements as redundant.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — FRE 807 · Dallas County v. Commercial Union Assurance Co. · United States v. Laster

q: Which statement about the scope of the Confrontation Clause is correct?
o: It protects only criminal defendants, and prosecution evidence must clear both the Clause and the hearsay rules.
It protects any party in a civil or criminal case against whom testimonial hearsay is offered.
It replaces the hearsay rules in criminal cases, so prosecution evidence that satisfies the Clause is admissible.
It applies equally to evidence offered by the defense, so the government may object to defense hearsay on confrontation grounds.
It bars all hearsay offered against the accused unless the declarant testifies.
e: Rule: "In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the right . . . to be confronted with the witnesses against him." The right protects only criminal defendants and operates independently of the hearsay rules.
oe: Correct. The slides' two preliminary points: the right belongs only to criminal defendants, and the hearsay rules and the Clause are separate hurdles. It applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment (Pointer v. Texas).
The right belongs only to the accused "in all criminal prosecutions." Civil litigants and the government have no confrontation right.
The hearsay rules and the Clause are separate exclusionary principles. Prosecution evidence must survive both.
The government has no confrontation right. Its objections to defense evidence rest on the hearsay rules.
After Crawford and Bockting, the Clause reaches only testimonial hearsay; nontestimonial statements face only the hearsay rules.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Sixth Amendment · Crawford v. Washington

q:
In a recorded, Mirandized stationhouse interview, a defendant's wife gives an account undermining his self-defense claim. She does not testify, because state law lets the defendant bar her testimony. The trial court admits her statement as against her penal interest and finds it reliable because it "interlocks" with his own statement.

Why did the Supreme Court reverse in Crawford?
o: Because a statement against penal interest is not a firmly rooted hearsay exception.
Because the wife's statement was unreliable under the totality of the circumstances.
Because the marital privilege made her unavailable, and unavailability alone bars admission.
Because the state court misapplied its own hearsay rule on statements against interest.
Because the statement was testimonial and he never had an opportunity to cross-examine her.
e: Rule: Testimonial statements of a witness who does not appear at trial are inadmissible unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity for cross-examination (Crawford). Roberts's reliability test no longer governs testimonial statements.
oe: That would have been a Roberts-era argument. Crawford overruled Roberts's reliability framework for testimonial statements.
Chief Justice Rehnquist would have decided on that ground, but the majority rejected reliability as the test: it is "an amorphous, if not entirely subjective, concept."
Unavailability is one requirement for admission, not a bar. What was missing was a prior opportunity for cross.
The state-law hearsay question was one the Supreme Court could not review ("CAN'T TOUCH," the slides say). The decision rested on the Constitution.

Correct. Police interrogations are core testimonial statements. "Dispensing with confrontation because testimony is obviously reliable is akin to dispensing with jury trial because a defendant is obviously guilty."
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Crawford v. Washington · Ohio v. Roberts

q: In which situation does the Confrontation Clause bar a prosecution witness's out-of-court testimonial statement?
o: The declarant testifies at trial and is cross-examined about the statement, though she now denies making it.
The declarant testifies at trial but claims she cannot remember the events described in the statement.
She has died, and the statement was a sworn affidavit to police that he never had a chance to cross-examine.
The statement is offered only to show that police had a reason to investigate the defendant, not for its truth.
The declarant has died, and the statement was testimony at a preliminary hearing at which the defendant cross-examined her.
e: Rule: The Clause is no bar when the statement is not offered for its truth, when the declarant testifies and is cross-examined (even with memory loss), when the declarant is unavailable and there was a prior opportunity for cross, when the defendant forfeited the right, or when the statement is nontestimonial.
oe: Green and Crawford footnote 9: when the declarant appears for cross-examination at trial, the Clause places no constraints on her prior statements.
Owens: a witness who takes the stand and answers questions is subject to cross-examination despite memory loss.
Correct. An affidavit to police is core testimonial hearsay. Death makes her unavailable, but without a prior opportunity for cross the statement is barred.
Crawford footnote 9: the Clause does not bar statements offered for purposes other than their truth. (Basis evidence relied on for its truth is different: Smith v. Arizona.)
Mattox and Crawford: prior testimony subject to cross is admissible if the declarant is unavailable.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Crawford v. Washington · California v. Green · United States v. Owens

q: Which statement is most likely nontestimonial under the primary-purpose test of Davis and Hammon?
o: A woman's written affidavit, signed on her porch after police separated her from her husband, describing how he had beaten her an hour earlier.
A woman's frantic answers to a 911 operator's questions while her ex-boyfriend is attacking her, including his name.
A man's answers to detectives at the station, after Miranda warnings, about a robbery that happened the day before.
A victim's description to an officer, given an hour after the assailant was arrested, of how the assault happened.
A sworn statement a witness gives a prosecutor while preparing for a grand jury appearance.
e: Rule: Statements in police interrogation are nontestimonial when circumstances objectively indicate that the primary purpose is to enable police assistance to meet an ongoing emergency; they are testimonial when there is no such emergency and the primary purpose is to establish or prove past events potentially relevant to a later prosecution (Davis).
oe: That is Hammon: the emergency was over, she described past events, and the questioning was structured. Testimonial.
Correct. That is Davis: she described events as they happened in a call for help, and the primary purpose of the interrogation was to enable police to meet an ongoing emergency.
Calm, formal, stationhouse questioning about past events is core testimonial interrogation.
With the assailant in custody, there is no ongoing emergency, and the statement describes past events.
Statements made for use in a prosecution are core testimonial statements.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Davis v. Washington · Hammon v. Indiana

q:
Police responding to a dispatch find a man mortally wounded in a gas-station parking lot. In answer to their questions, he says "Rick" shot him through the back door of Rick's house six blocks away, about 25 minutes earlier. The shooter's whereabouts are unknown.

Why did the Supreme Court hold the statements nontestimonial?
o: Because the declarant died, and dying declarations are categorically outside the Confrontation Clause.
Because its objective primary purpose was to meet an ongoing emergency: an armed shooter at large.
Because the officers subjectively intended to help the victim rather than gather evidence.
Because statements made outside a police station are never testimonial.
Because the victim's statements were reliable excited utterances, and reliable statements satisfy the Clause.
e: Rule: Whether an ongoing emergency exists depends on the type and scope of the threat. Courts consider the statements and actions of both the declarant and the interrogators, the formality of the encounter, the location, and the declarant's medical condition, judged objectively.
oe: No dying-declaration foundation was laid at trial, and the Court did not rest on that ground.
Correct. The emergency's scope depends on the threat: unlike Davis and Hammon, this was not a domestic dispute, it involved a gun, and the shooter could threaten police and the public.
The test is objective: the purpose "reasonable participants would have had," not the officers' actual subjective purposes.
Location is one factor among several, not a categorical rule. Hammon's statements were made at home and were testimonial.
Reliability is relevant to the primary-purpose inquiry (Sotomayor, J.), but reliability alone does not satisfy the Clause; Crawford rejected that approach.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Michigan v. Bryant

q:
At a DWI trial, the prosecution introduces a signed lab certificate reporting the defendant's blood-alcohol level. The analyst who ran the test is on leave. Instead, a different analyst from the same lab, who did not observe or review the test, explains the lab's procedures.

Under Bullcoming, does this satisfy the Confrontation Clause?
o: Yes, because the certificate was unsworn and therefore not testimonial.
No, because a surrogate analyst cannot stand in for the analyst who certified the result.
Yes, because lab results are neutral, scientific records like business records.
No, because the Clause requires the prosecution to call every lab employee who handled the sample.
Yes, because the defendant could have subpoenaed the original analyst himself.
e: Rule: Sworn or certified forensic reports created for use at trial are testimonial (Melendez-Diaz). The prosecution may not satisfy the Clause with a surrogate analyst who did not perform or observe the test (Bullcoming).
oe: Bullcoming held the certificate formal enough to be testimonial: it was created solely for an evidentiary purpose, in aid of a police investigation.
Correct. "The accused's right is to be confronted with the analyst who made the certification." The certificate reported more than machine output, and gas chromatography is vulnerable to human error.
Melendez-Diaz rejected that argument: documents prepared for use at trial are not ordinary business records, and analysts are "witnesses against" the defendant.
Neither case requires every person in the chain of custody to testify. The issue is the analyst who made the testimonial certification.
Melendez-Diaz held that the defendant's subpoena power does not satisfy the Clause, though states may adopt notice-and-demand statutes.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts · Bullcoming v. New Mexico

q:
At a drug trial, the analyst who tested the seized substances has left the lab. A substitute expert reviews her notes and report, tells the jury what they say, and gives his "independent opinion" that the substances were methamphetamine. The state argues that the absent analyst's statements came in only as the basis of the expert's opinion, not for their truth.

What did the Supreme Court hold in Smith v. Arizona?
o: The testimony was proper, because under Rule 703 principles basis evidence is never offered for its truth.
The testimony violated the Clause, because lab notes and reports are always testimonial.
The testimony was proper, because the expert gave an independent opinion and was himself available for cross-examination.
Basis statements that support the opinion only if true are offered for their truth, so the Clause applies if testimonial.
The testimony violated the Clause, because any expert opinion based on hearsay is inadmissible in a criminal case.
e: Rule: When an expert conveys an absent analyst's statements in support of an opinion, and the statements provide that support only if true, they come into evidence for their truth (Smith v. Arizona). Whether they are testimonial is a separate question.
oe: That was the Williams plurality's theory and Arizona's reasoning. Smith rejected it for confrontation purposes.
Smith did not decide that. Whether the absent analyst's statements were testimonial was left for the state courts.
The expert's opinion was only as good as the analyst's statements, and cross of the substitute could not test them.
Correct. Smith held the statements were offered for their truth and remanded the testimonial question. A state's evidence-law label does not control the constitutional inquiry.
Experts may still rely on hearsay under Rule 703. The constitutional issue arises when they convey testimonial statements for their truth.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Smith v. Arizona · Williams v. Illinois · FRE 703

q:
A three-year-old with facial injuries tells his preschool teachers, in answer to their questions, that "Dee" hurt him. The teachers are mandatory reporters under state law. The child is found incompetent to testify, and his statements are offered at Dee's trial.

Which statement best reflects Ohio v. Clark?
o: The statements are testimonial, because a mandatory-reporting duty makes teachers agents of law enforcement.
The statements are testimonial, because the teachers' questions were aimed at identifying an abuser.
The statements are inadmissible, because a child found incompetent to testify cannot make admissible hearsay statements.
They are nontestimonial, because no one's primary purpose was to aid a prosecution, and the child was very young.
The statements are nontestimonial, because the Clause never applies to statements made to private persons.
e: Rule: A statement is testimonial when made with the primary purpose of creating an out-of-court substitute for trial testimony. Statements to persons not principally charged with uncovering and prosecuting crime are significantly less likely to be testimonial, and very young children's statements rarely will be (Clark).
oe: The Court rejected that view: "like all good teachers," they would have acted the same way without the duty.
The teachers needed to know whether it was safe to send the child home. The context was an ongoing emergency involving suspected child abuse.
Incompetency to testify does not bar hearsay. The statements came in under a state child-hearsay exception, and the Clause posed no bar.

Correct. The questioning was informal and spontaneous, statements to people not principally charged with uncovering crime are much less likely to be testimonial, and a three-year-old would not understand the prosecutorial use of his words.
Clark declined to adopt a categorical rule for statements to non-police, though such statements are "significantly less likely" to be testimonial.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Ohio v. Clark

q: Which statement about forfeiture and nontestimonial hearsay is correct?
o: A defendant forfeits his confrontation right whenever his own wrongdoing caused the declarant's absence, whatever his purpose.
The Confrontation Clause still requires nontestimonial hearsay to bear particularized guarantees of trustworthiness.
Forfeiture requires intent to silence the witness, and nontestimonial hearsay is outside the Clause.
Crawford applies retroactively on collateral review, so pre-2004 convictions resting on testimonial hearsay must be vacated.
A trial judge may admit testimonial hearsay to correct a misleading impression created by the defense, if necessary.
e: Rule: A defendant forfeits the confrontation right only by wrongdoing intended to prevent the witness from testifying (Giles). Nontestimonial statements are outside the Clause (Bockting).
oe: Giles requires that the defendant intended to prevent the witness from testifying. Murder alone is not enough unless preventing testimony was a purpose.
Bockting said Crawford eliminated Confrontation Clause protection against unreliable nontestimonial statements.
Correct. Giles constitutionalized the intent requirement of Rule 804(b)(6). Bockting confirmed that nontestimonial statements fall outside the Clause.
Bockting held that Crawford is not retroactive on collateral review.
Hemphill v. New York rejected a state "opening the door" doctrine for testimonial hearsay: the right is not subject to a judge's reliability or necessity assessment.
topic: Residual exception & Confrontation — Giles v. California · Whorton v. Bockting

q:
A prosecutor offers part of a recorded oral statement in which the defendant said, "I had the gun." The defendant wants the jury to hear his next sentence in the same statement: "but I took it from him after he pulled it on me."

Which statement correctly applies Rule 106, as amended in 2023?
o: The defendant may not require the completing statement, because Rule 106 applies only to writings and recordings, not oral statements.
The defendant may introduce it only during his own case, after the prosecution rests.
The defendant may require the entire statement, including unrelated parts, once any part is introduced.
The completing statement is inadmissible, because a defendant's self-serving statement is hearsay when he offers it.
He may require it at that time, over a hearsay objection, to correct the misleading impression.
e: Rule: If a party introduces all or part of a statement, an adverse party may require the introduction, at that time, of any other part, or any other statement, that in fairness ought to be considered at the same time, over a hearsay objection (FRE 106).
oe: The 2023 amendment extended Rule 106 to all statements, oral as well as written or recorded.
The adverse party may require introduction "at that time," without waiting for its own case.
"In fairness" limits the completing evidence to what is needed to correct a misleading impression, not everything said.
That is the problem the 2023 amendment solved: the completing portion is admissible over a hearsay objection.
Correct. Since 2023, the completing portion comes in over a hearsay objection, and its timing is immediate. Only what fairness requires to correct a distortion comes in.
topic: Completeness, Bruton & right to a defense — FRE 106

q:
Two defendants are tried jointly before one jury. A postal inspector testifies that one defendant, Evans, confessed that he and his codefendant, Bruton, committed the robbery. Evans does not testify. The judge clearly instructs the jury to consider the confession only against Evans.

Which statement reflects the Supreme Court's holding?
o: It violated Bruton's confrontation right, because the instruction could not adequately protect him.
The instruction cured any problem, because juries are presumed to follow limiting instructions.
The confession was admissible against Bruton as a statement against Evans's penal interest.
The problem could not have been avoided except by severing the trials.
The confession would have been admissible against Bruton if Evans had testified and denied making it.
e: Rule: Admitting a nontestifying codefendant's confession that facially incriminates another defendant in a joint trial violates that defendant's Confrontation Clause rights, even with a limiting instruction (Bruton).
oe: Correct. Powerfully incriminating statements of a codefendant, deliberately spread before the jury and inherently suspect, cannot be cured by instruction: "The effect is the same as if there had been no instruction at all."
Bruton overruled Delli Paoli on this point: in this context, the instruction is not an adequate substitute for cross-examination.
Footnote 3: the statement was "clearly inadmissible against [Bruton] under traditional rules of evidence." Bruton starts from that premise.
Prosecutors have several alternatives: separate juries, a testifying codefendant, prior cross-examined testimony, redaction, or a bench trial.
If Evans testified and was cross-examined, there would be no confrontation problem (Nelson v. O'Neil), but that does not make the confession admissible against Bruton for its truth.
topic: Completeness, Bruton & right to a defense — Bruton v. United States

q: A codefendant's confession to police is to be read at a joint trial. Which version is most likely to violate the Confrontation Clause, even with a limiting instruction?
o: A version redacted to remove the defendant's name and any reference to his existence, which becomes incriminating only when linked with later evidence.
A version in which the defendant's name is replaced with a neutral descriptor, "the other person he was with."
A version made by a codefendant who testifies at trial and is cross-examined about the confession.
A version in which the defendant's name is replaced with the word "deleted," as in "Me, deleted, deleted, and a few other guys."
A version consisting of a coconspirator's nontestimonial statement made during and in furtherance of the conspiracy.
e: Rule: Redaction that eliminates the defendant's name and any reference to his existence avoids Bruton (Richardson). Replacing the name with an obvious deletion does not (Gray). A natural neutral descriptor is permitted (Samia).
oe: Richardson v. Marsh held there is no violation when the confession is redacted to eliminate not only the name but any reference to the defendant's existence.
Samia (2023) held that a neutral descriptor read naturally, with a limiting instruction, does not violate the Clause.
A testifying codefendant raises no confrontation problem.
Correct. Gray held that redaction replacing a name with an obvious indication of deletion, such as a blank or the word "deleted," still falls within Bruton's rule, as a class.
A nontestimonial coconspirator statement is admissible against the defendant too, so there is no Bruton problem.
topic: Completeness, Bruton & right to a defense — Bruton v. United States · Richardson · Gray v. Maryland · Samia v. United States

q:
At a joint trial, the prosecution offers a codefendant's boast to his cellmate, a friend, that "Tony and I did the job." The codefendant does not testify. Tony raises a Bruton objection.

What is the best analysis after Crawford?
o: Bruton bars the statement, because any codefendant's statement incriminating another defendant in a joint trial violates the Clause.
Bruton bars the statement unless it is redacted to remove Tony's name with a blank.
Bruton does not apply to a nontestimonial remark, so only hearsay rules, Rule 403, and severance remain.
The statement is admissible against Tony as the codefendant's own statement under Rule 801(d)(2)(A).
The statement is admissible against Tony under Rule 801(d)(2)(E), because codefendants are always coconspirators.
e: Rule: Bruton's elements: a nontestifying codefendant's statement, a joint trial before one jury, inadmissible against the defendant, facially incriminating, and (after Crawford) testimonial.
oe: After Crawford, circuits hold that Bruton applies only to testimonial statements.
A blank would itself raise a Gray problem if Bruton applied. But Bruton does not apply to nontestimonial statements.
Correct. Without a testimonial statement there is no confrontation violation and so no Bruton problem. The statement must still fit a hearsay exception against Tony.
A party's own statement is admissible only against that party. Against Tony, the codefendant's statement needs its own exception.
A boast after the fact to a cellmate is not "during and in furtherance" of a conspiracy.
topic: Completeness, Bruton & right to a defense — Bruton v. United States · Crawford v. Washington

q:
A defendant charged with murdering a police officer calls the man he claims was the real shooter, who had signed a sworn confession and then repudiated it. The State's voucher rule prevents the defendant from cross-examining him, and the hearsay rule (which recognizes only pecuniary, not penal, interest) excludes his three oral confessions to friends.

Why did the Supreme Court reverse the conviction in Chambers?
o: Because excluding critical, trustworthy defense evidence while barring his cross denied due process.
Because the Confrontation Clause gives a defendant the right to cross-examine any witness he calls.
Because the Federal Rules of Evidence would have admitted the oral confessions under Rule 804(b)(3).
Because a state may never exclude a confession against penal interest offered by a defendant.
Because the jury was all white and the trial took place in a racially tense community.
e: Rule: Where constitutional rights directly affecting the ascertainment of guilt are implicated, the hearsay rule may not be applied mechanistically to defeat the ends of justice; excluding critical and trustworthy defense evidence can deny due process (Chambers).
oe: Correct. The confessions were made spontaneously to close acquaintances shortly after the crime, corroborated, against interest, and the declarant was available for cross by the State. "The hearsay rule may not be applied mechanistically to defeat the ends of justice."
The voucher-rule restriction was part of the problem, but the holding rested on due process as applied to the combination of rulings.
The Federal Rules would not have admitted them under 804(b)(3), because the declarant was available.
The Court declined to decide whether the pecuniary-only rule is valid "under other circumstances" and said it established "no new principles of constitutional law."
Those facts are context, not the holding.
topic: Completeness, Bruton & right to a defense — Chambers v. Mississippi

q: Which defense challenge to an exclusionary rule is most likely to succeed under the right to present a complete defense?
o: A challenge to a per se military rule excluding all polygraph evidence, by a defendant who passed a polygraph.
A challenge to a statute barring jurors from considering voluntary intoxication on mens rea.
A challenge to an ordinary rule excluding third-party-guilt evidence that raises only a "bare suspicion."
A challenge to a rule barring third-party-guilt evidence whenever the State's forensic case is strong.
A challenge to a witness's valid invocation of the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.
e: Rule: The Constitution guarantees criminal defendants "a meaningful opportunity to present a complete defense" (Crane). Rules that are arbitrary or disproportionate to their purposes (Washington, Rock, Holmes), or valid rules applied mechanistically to exclude critical, trustworthy evidence (Chambers), violate it.
oe: United States v. Scheffer upheld that ban as neither arbitrary nor disproportionate.
Montana v. Egelhoff upheld such a statute, calling Chambers "an exercise in highly case-specific error correction."
Holmes said ordinary third-party-guilt rules of that kind, like Rule 403, are constitutional.
Correct. Holmes v. South Carolina held that rule arbitrary: judging the defense evidence only by the strength of the prosecution's case says nothing about the strength of the defense evidence.
A witness's Fifth Amendment privilege almost always prevails over a defendant's compulsory-process claim.
topic: Completeness, Bruton & right to a defense — Chambers v. Mississippi · right to present a defense

q: Which testimony is proper lay opinion under Rule 701?
o: An officer with no special training testifies that the defendant's car was traveling 37 miles per hour, based on skid-mark calculations he learned from a manual.
A detective testifies, as a lay witness, what drug traffickers' coded words mean based on years of narcotics investigations.
A former drug user identifies marijuana's country of origin from its appearance and the "high" it produces.
A neighbor who saw the defendant shortly before a crash testifies that he "seemed drunk," after describing his slurred speech and swaying.
A witness who did not see the accident testifies that the driver was "probably negligent."
e: Rule: A lay opinion must be (a) rationally based on the witness's perception, (b) helpful to understanding the testimony or determining a fact in issue, and (c) not based on scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge within Rule 702 (FRE 701).
oe: Reconstructing speed from skid marks rests on technical knowledge within Rule 702, so it is barred as lay opinion by 701(c).
Interpreting drug argot from experience is specialized knowledge. Offering it as lay opinion would be "an expert in lay witness clothing."
A familiar substance's identity can be lay opinion, but its country of origin rests on specialized knowledge, so it is expert testimony (Problem 9.5).
Correct. Intoxication, after a foundation of observed facts, is classic lay opinion: rationally based on perception and helpful to the jury.
The opinion is not based on the witness's perception, and it states a legal conclusion that does not help the jury.
topic: Lay & expert opinion, reliability — FRE 701

q: Which expert testimony is most likely permissible?
