o: In an excessive-force suit, a police-practices expert testifies that the officer's blow was "deadly physical force" that was "not justified under the circumstances."
In a drug-courier prosecution, an expert testifies that this defendant knew she was carrying drugs.
In a will contest, an expert testifies simply that the testator "lacked capacity to make a will."
In a drug-courier prosecution, an expert testifies that most couriers know they are carrying drugs.
In a fraud case, an expert explains to the jury what the elements of securities fraud are.
e: Rule: An opinion is not objectionable just because it embraces an ultimate issue (FRE 704(a)). But in a criminal case an expert may not state an opinion about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state that is an element of the crime or a defense (FRE 704(b)).
oe: Hygh v. Jacobs held such testimony must be excluded: it states legal conclusions and tells the jury what result to reach.
Rule 704(b) bars an expert from stating an opinion about whether the defendant had a mental state that is an element of the crime.
The ACN's example: that question uses inadequately explored legal criteria. The expert may testify in terms of the underlying elements of capacity instead.
Correct. Diaz v. United States (2024) held that Rule 704(b) bars only opinions about the particular defendant's mental state, not opinions about most people in her position.
Instructing the jury on the law is the judge's role. An expert may not do it.
topic: Lay & expert opinion, reliability — FRE 704 · Hygh v. Jacobs · Diaz v. United States

q: Which expert testimony is most likely admissible?
o: A psychologist who interviewed a child complainant testifies that, in his professional judgment, she was telling the truth.
A psychologist explains that delayed reporting and recantation are common, without discussing this child.
An eyewitness-identification expert testifies that the prosecution's eyewitness was probably mistaken.
A defense expert testifies that the officers were not lying because a lie would have been easily disproved.
A rap scholar testifies that the defendant's specific lyrics were fictional and did not describe real events.
e: Rule: Expert testimony must help the trier of fact (FRE 702(a)). An expert may explain counterintuitive behavior or general factors affecting reliability, but may not vouch for or against a particular witness's credibility.
oe: Batangan held that an expert may not give a conclusory opinion that the child is truthful or was abused; jurors judge credibility.
Correct. Batangan allows experts to explain "seemingly bizarre" behavior, even though doing so incidentally bolsters credibility.
Guilbert allows testimony on general factors affecting identification but not an opinion about whether a particular eyewitness is accurate.
Nimely (Problem 9.11) held that such an opinion on officers' truthfulness usurps the jury's role.
General testimony about genre conventions may be acceptable, but an opinion that these lyrics are false is credibility vouching (Problem 9.12).
topic: Lay & expert opinion, reliability — FRE 702 · State v. Batangan · State v. Guilbert

q:
A stranger to the defendant identified him as a shooter after seeing his photo in a newspaper ten days later. The defense offers an expert on the weak link between confidence and accuracy, the effects of stress, and postevent information. The trial court excludes the expert as testifying to common knowledge and gives a cautionary instruction instead.

What did the Connecticut Supreme Court hold in Guilbert?
o: The exclusion was proper, because cross-examination and jury instructions adequately expose eyewitness errors.
The exclusion was proper, because eyewitness expertise fails the reliability standards of Rule 702.
Such experts are admissible when helpful; excluding this one as to the stranger was error, though harmless.
The expert may testify that the stranger's identification was probably wrong, given the newspaper photo.
Strong corroborating evidence always justifies excluding such an expert.
e: Rule: Expert testimony on the fallibility of eyewitness identification is admissible when it would help the jury, subject to qualification, relevance, and reliability screening and the trial court's discretion (Guilbert).
oe: Guilbert rejected this: cross exposes lies better than sincere mistakes, and generalized instructions come too late and say too little.
The court found the research reliable and widely accepted, reflected in a near-national consensus.

Correct. Guilbert overruled earlier cases treating the subject as common knowledge. As to the four witnesses who knew the defendant, there was no abuse; as to the stranger there was, but the error was harmless.
The expert may describe general factors but may not opine on whether a particular eyewitness is accurate.
The majority said corroboration does not justify exclusion; it bears on harmlessness. The concurrence would have let trial courts weigh it.
topic: Lay & expert opinion, reliability — FRE 702 · State v. Guilbert

q:
In a civil-commitment hearing, a psychiatrist's opinion that the respondent is dangerous rests largely on the respondent's mother's report that he punched her. The mother does not testify, and her report is inadmissible hearsay.

Which statement is correct?
o: The opinion may come in, but disclosing the mother's report requires passing Rule 703's reverse-403 test.
The opinion is inadmissible, because an expert's opinion must rest on admissible evidence.
The opinion and the mother's report are both admissible for their truth, because the expert relied on the report.
The report may be disclosed freely, because a limiting instruction will tell the jury not to consider it for its truth.
The opinion is admissible only if the expert first testifies to all the underlying facts on direct.
e: Rule: An expert may base an opinion on facts or data that experts in the field would reasonably rely on, even if inadmissible; but the proponent may disclose inadmissible facts or data only if their probative value in helping the jury evaluate the opinion substantially outweighs their prejudicial effect (FRE 703).
oe: Correct. Melton found psychiatrists reasonably rely on family reports. Rule 703's reverse-403 test creates a presumption against disclosure of inadmissible bases by the proponent.
Rule 703: if experts in the field would reasonably rely on that kind of data, it need not be admissible for the opinion to be admitted.
Reliance does not make the underlying facts admissible. Only the opinion comes in.
Melton: "Labels cannot perform juridical alchemy." The jury cannot evaluate the opinion without believing the punch happened, which is why disclosure is restricted.
Rule 705 lets an expert state an opinion and reasons without first testifying to the underlying facts, unless the court orders otherwise.
topic: Lay & expert opinion, reliability — FRE 703 · FRE 705 · In re Melton

q: Which statement about Daubert is correct?
o: It makes the judge a gatekeeper who screens reliability and fit under 104(a), using flexible factors.
Daubert adopted Frye's general-acceptance test as the exclusive standard for scientific evidence under Rule 702.
Daubert directs the judge to decide whether the expert's conclusions are correct.
Daubert applies only in federal criminal cases and binds the states through due process.
Daubert held that an expert's opinion is admissible whenever the expert is qualified, leaving reliability to the jury.
e: Rule: Under Rule 702, the trial judge must ensure that expert testimony is relevant and reliable, as a preliminary question under 104(a). Daubert's non-exclusive factors are testability, peer review and publication, the known or potential error rate, standards controlling the technique, and general acceptance.
oe: Correct. The factors are non-exclusive, the inquiry is "a flexible one," and shaky but admissible evidence is met by cross-examination, contrary evidence, and instructions.
Daubert held that Frye did not survive the Federal Rules. General acceptance is one factor, not the test.
The focus "must be solely on principles and methodology, not on the conclusions that they generate" (though Joiner later said the two are not entirely distinct).
Daubert interprets Federal Rule 702 and binds no state; Fisher counts 31 Daubert states and 6 Frye states.
Daubert requires the judge to ensure reliability as a preliminary question; qualification alone is not enough.
topic: Lay & expert opinion, reliability — FRE 702 · Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc. · Frye v. United States

q: Which statement about the rest of the Daubert trilogy is correct?
o: Kumho Tire held that Daubert's gatekeeping applies only to scientific testimony, not to engineers or experience-based experts.
Joiner lets courts reject opinions resting on ipse dixit, and Kumho extends gatekeeping to all experts.
Kumho Tire requires the trial judge to apply all five Daubert factors to every expert.
Joiner held that appellate courts review a trial judge's reliability ruling de novo.
Kumho Tire held that an experienced expert's visual inspection of a tire is reliable as a matter of law.
e: Rule: Conclusions and methodology are not entirely distinct; a court may exclude an opinion when there is too great an analytical gap between the data and the opinion (Joiner). The gatekeeping obligation applies to all expert testimony, and the Daubert factors may be used where they fit (Kumho).
oe: Kumho held the opposite: the gatekeeping duty applies to all expert testimony, "scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge."
Correct. Joiner: "too great an analytical gap between the data and the opinion proffered." Kumho: the judge has the same latitude in deciding how to test reliability as in deciding whether it exists.
The judge "may" use the factors where they are reasonable measures of reliability; they are neither required nor ruled out for any category of expert.
Joiner set abuse-of-discretion review.
Kumho asked whether this expert's method could reliably distinguish abuse from defect on this tire, and upheld exclusion.
topic: Lay & expert opinion, reliability — General Electric Co. v. Joiner · Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael

q: Which statement best describes current law on expert reliability and forensic testimony?
o: Under the 2023 amendment, questions about an expert's basis and methodology always go to weight, for the jury.
After the National Academy of Sciences report, courts routinely exclude fingerprint evidence as unscientific.
The PCAST report found bitemark analysis foundationally valid when performed by board-certified examiners.
Each 702 element must be shown to the court by a preponderance, and forensic claims are usually limited.
Polygraph evidence is now generally admissible under Daubert because it has a known error rate.
e: Rule: Since Dec. 1, 2023, the proponent must demonstrate to the court that it is more likely than not that the expert's knowledge will help, the testimony rests on sufficient facts or data, it is the product of reliable methods, and the opinion reflects a reliable application of those methods (FRE 702).
oe: The amendment clarified the opposite: the proponent must demonstrate each requirement to the court by a preponderance.
Courts acknowledged the report and admitted the evidence anyway, sometimes with limits (United States v. Council).
PCAST found bitemark analysis not valid, with false-positive rates often above 10%, and courts are pushing it out.

Correct. The 2023 amendment wrote the preponderance standard into 702 and stresses that each opinion must stay within what a reliable application supports. Courts typically limit, rather than exclude, fields like firearms and fingerprints.
Polygraph evidence remains excluded almost everywhere unless the parties stipulate, and Scheffer upheld a per se ban.
topic: Lay & expert opinion, reliability — FRE 702 (2023 amendment) · forensic science

q: Which statement about authentication is correct?
o: The judge must find by a preponderance that the exhibit is what its proponent claims before admitting it.
Once an exhibit is authenticated, it is admissible, because authentication resolves all objections to it.
There must be evidence sufficient for a reasonable jury to find authenticity, and the jury then decides.
Self-authenticating documents under Rule 902 may not be challenged as forgeries.
The 901(b) examples are an exclusive list of permissible methods of authentication.
e: Rule: To authenticate or identify an item of evidence, the proponent must produce evidence sufficient to support a finding that the item is what the proponent claims it is (FRE 901(a)).
oe: Authentication is conditional relevance. The judge asks only whether there is evidence sufficient to support a finding.
Authentication is only the first gate. The exhibit may still fail on hearsay, the best evidence rule, or 403.
Correct. Rule 901(a) tracks Rule 104(b) and Huddleston. The judge screens, the jury decides, and the opponent may argue the exhibit is not genuine.
Rule 902 dispenses with extrinsic evidence of authenticity, but the opponent may still dispute authenticity before the jury.
The examples are "examples only—not a complete list."
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 901(a) · FRE 104(b)

q: The prosecution needs to prove that the defendant wrote a ransom note. Which method of authentication is least likely to be permitted?
o: The defendant's sister, who has seen his handwriting on birthday cards for twenty years, testifies that the note is in his hand.
A forensic document examiner compares the note with the defendant's authenticated exemplars and testifies they match.
A paralegal who studied the defendant's writing only for this trial gives a lay opinion that the note is his.
The jury compares the note with authenticated samples of the defendant's handwriting itself.
The note contains details about the victim's family that only the defendant would likely know.
e: Rule: A nonexpert's opinion that handwriting is genuine must be based on familiarity not acquired for the current litigation (FRE 901(b)(2)); an expert or the trier of fact may compare the item with an authenticated specimen (FRE 901(b)(3)).
oe: Lay familiarity acquired in ordinary life is the paradigm of 901(b)(2).
Expert comparison with an authenticated specimen is permitted by 901(b)(3).
Correct. Rule 901(b)(2) requires that a nonexpert's familiarity with the handwriting not be "acquired for the current litigation."
Rule 901(b)(3) allows comparison "by an expert witness or the trier of fact."
Distinctive contents, taken together with all the circumstances, can authenticate a writing under 901(b)(4).
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 901(b)(2) · FRE 901(b)(3)

q:
The prosecution offers incriminating text messages sent from a phone registered to the defendant. The defendant says others sometimes used his phone.

What is the best statement of the authentication requirement under Benton?
o: Proof that the defendant owned the phone is enough to authenticate any message sent from it.
Text messages may be authenticated only by testimony of a person who saw the defendant type them.
Text messages are self-authenticating under Rule 902 if extracted by forensic software.
There must be evidence that he wrote them, which content, timing, and context can supply.
Social-media and text messages require a heightened standard of authentication beyond Rule 901(a).
e: Rule: Authenticating text messages, posts, and emails requires evidence of authorship, not just ownership of the device or account; content, timing, context, and background knowledge can supply it under 901(b)(4) (Benton).
oe: Benton held that authenticating texts "requires more than proving mere ownership of the device."
Circumstantial evidence under 901(b)(4) suffices; an eyewitness to the typing is not required.
Rule 902(14) can authenticate data copied from a device by digital identification, but that proves the copy is accurate, not who wrote the messages.
Correct. Benton found the texts authenticated circumstantially: the phone carried the defendant's steady personal texts alongside the planning messages.
No heightened standard applies (compare Oreckinto on internet evidence). The ordinary standard is applied to the authorship question.
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 901(b)(4) · State v. Benton

q:
A homeowner's security company installed and periodically serviced a continuously recording camera system. The system recorded a burglary while the homeowner was away. He did not see the burglary and knows nothing about how the system works internally.

May the homeowner lay the foundation for the video?
o: No, because a video may be authenticated only by a witness who saw the events and testifies it fairly and accurately depicts them.
No, because only the technician who installed the system can testify that it produces accurate results.
Yes, but only if the video is self-authenticating under Rule 902(13) by a certification.
Yes, because security videos are presumed authentic unless the opponent proves tampering.
Yes, under a silent-witness theory, by describing the system's history, reliability, and the download.
e: Rule: Photos and videos may be authenticated by a witness with knowledge that they fairly and accurately show what the witness saw (901(b)(1)), or, with no eyewitness, by evidence that the recording process produces an accurate result (901(b)(9)).
oe: That is the "pictorial testimony" theory. When no one saw the events, the "silent witness" theory under 901(b)(9) is available.
Luke rejected a rigid requirement of technical testimony. A regular user's testimony can suffice.
Rule 902(13) is one option, but live testimony by a user is enough under 901.
There is no presumption. The proponent must still offer evidence sufficient to support a finding.
Correct. Luke held that the user's testimony supported a reasonable inference that the video was what it purported to be. His lack of firsthand or technical knowledge went to weight.
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 901(b)(1) · FRE 901(b)(9) · State v. Luke

q:
Police seize a bag of white powder from the defendant, place it in a locked evidence safe, and send it to the lab. At trial, the prosecution cannot account for one day during which the bag was in the lab's general intake area. There is no evidence of tampering.

Which statement is correct?
o: The powder is inadmissible, because the chain of custody for fungible evidence must be unbroken.
The powder is admissible without any chain of custody, because a witness can recognize the bag.
It is admissible if a jury could find it is the same substance in substantially the same condition.
The powder is inadmissible unless every person who handled it testifies, by analogy to Melendez-Diaz.
The powder is inadmissible unless the prosecution proves by clear and convincing evidence that no tampering occurred.
e: Rule: A unique item can be identified by a witness who recognizes it; a fungible item requires a chain of custody. Gaps in the chain usually go to weight, and the test is whether the evidence supports a finding that the item is the same, in substantially the same condition.
oe: The chain need not be perfect. A gap usually goes to weight, not admissibility.
Unless the bag is uniquely marked, an officer cannot reliably recognize a packet of white powder; that is why fungible items need a chain.
Correct. A fungible item needs a chain of custody, but courts ask whether a reasonable jury could find it is the same substance in substantially the same condition.
Neither the authentication rules nor Melendez-Diaz requires every person in the chain to testify.
No heightened standard applies; the 104(b)-type sufficiency standard governs.
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 901(a) · chain of custody

q:
In 2026, the government offers wartime documents from a foreign archive, found where such records would be kept and showing no signs of alteration, to prove the defendant's service in a military unit in 1941.

Which statement is correct?
o: The documents are authenticated as ancient documents, and for that reason they are also admissible for their truth under the ancient-documents hearsay exception.
They are authenticated under 901(b)(8) and, being pre-1998, also fit 803(16), but the rules are separate hurdles.
The documents cannot be authenticated without a strict chain of custody from 1941 to trial.
Rule 803(16) covers any document at least 20 years old, so a document prepared in 2000 also qualifies.
The documents are self-authenticating as foreign public documents without any further showing.
e: Rule: A document is authenticated as ancient if its condition creates no suspicion about its authenticity, it was in a place where it would likely be, and it is at least 20 years old (FRE 901(b)(8)). The hearsay exception for ancient documents covers only documents prepared before Jan. 1, 1998 whose authenticity is established (FRE 803(16)).
oe: Authentication and hearsay are separate hurdles; satisfying one does not satisfy the other.
Correct. Since 2017, 803(16) covers only documents prepared before Jan. 1, 1998 whose authenticity is established, while 901(b)(8)'s 20-year rule is unchanged. These 1941 documents satisfy both.
Stelmokas held no strict chain of custody was required for ancient documents.
That was the pre-2017 rule. A document prepared in 2000 fits 901(b)(8) but not 803(16).
Rule 902(3) requires a final certification. Stelmokas relied on 901(b)(8) and historians' testimony.
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 901(b)(8) · FRE 803(16) · United States v. Stelmokas

q: Which item is self-authenticating under Rule 902, requiring no extrinsic evidence of authenticity?
o: A business record with a certification meeting 803(6)(A)–(C), after advance written notice.
A photograph of a crime scene, offered with no testimony about who took it.
A private letter bearing the purported signature of the defendant.
An email printout offered with a statement from the recipient that it came from the defendant.
A handwritten inventory list found in the defendant's garage, offered with no testimony about who wrote it.
e: Rule: Self-authenticating items include certified and sealed public documents, certified copies of public records, official publications, newspapers and periodicals, trade inscriptions, notarized documents, commercial paper, and certified business and electronic records with notice (FRE 902).
oe: Correct. Rule 902(11) makes certified domestic business records self-authenticating if the proponent gives reasonable written notice and makes the record available for inspection.
Photographs are not self-authenticating. A witness must testify that it fairly depicts the scene, or the process must be shown accurate.
A private letter needs authentication under 901, for example by handwriting or distinctive contents.
The recipient's statement is extrinsic evidence under 901; emails are not self-authenticating.
An unsigned private writing is not on the 902 list. It needs authentication under 901, for example by handwriting comparison or distinctive contents.
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 902

q: In which situation does the best evidence rule require the original or an excuse for its absence?
o: A bank teller testifies from memory about a robbery, though a surveillance tape of the robbery exists.
A witness testifies from memory to what a defendant said under oath at an earlier hearing, without the transcript.
A witness describes the knife found in the robber's sock.
A neighbor testifies from memory to the license number she saw on a car.
An officer describes what a boat's GPS data showed without producing the device or a printout.
e: Rule: An original writing, recording, or photograph is required to prove its content unless the rules or a statute provide otherwise (FRE 1002). Other evidence of content is admissible if the originals are lost or destroyed (not by the proponent in bad faith), unobtainable, in the opponent's control after notice, or not closely related to a controlling issue (FRE 1004).
oe: The teller is proving what he saw, not the contents of the tape. The rule does not require the "best" evidence on every point.
The thing proved is the testimony itself, an event, not the transcript's content (Meyers).
The rule applies only to writings, recordings, and photographs, not objects.
She proves what she saw. Inscribed objects like plates are treated flexibly, and a simple number carries little risk of the errors the rule targets.
Correct. The officer was proving the content of a recording, so Rule 1002 required the original or a 1004 excuse (United States v. Bennett, reversed).
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 1002 · FRE 1004

q: Which statement about originals, duplicates, and excuses is correct?
o: A copy made by hand by a careful clerk is a "duplicate" admissible like the original.
A duplicate is never admissible if the opponent objects.
A printout of electronically stored information is a copy, not an original, under Rule 1001.
In a jury trial, the judge alone decides whether a disputed writing ever existed.
An artist who lost his originals in bad faith may not prove them by later reconstructions.
e: Rule: An "original" includes any counterpart intended to have the same effect and any accurate printout of electronic data; a duplicate is an accurate mechanical or electronic reproduction, admissible like the original unless its authenticity is genuinely questioned or admission would be unfair (FRE 1001, 1003). Bad-faith loss by the proponent defeats the 1004(a) excuse.
oe: Duplicates must be produced by an accurate mechanical, photographic, chemical, or electronic process. Handmade copies risk transcription error.
A duplicate is admissible like the original unless there is a genuine question about the original's authenticity or admission would be unfair (1003).
For electronically stored information, any printout or readable output that accurately reflects it is an "original."
Under Rule 1008, the jury decides whether the writing ever existed, whether another one is the original, and whether other evidence of content is accurate.
Correct. Seiler held that drawings are "writings," the contents were at issue, and 1004(a) does not excuse originals lost or destroyed by the proponent in bad faith.
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 1001 · FRE 1003 · FRE 1004 · Seiler v. Lucasfilm, Ltd.

q:
A detective found internet images of a commercially available hooded sweatshirt with distinctive lettering through a search engine, but cannot identify the websites. The prosecution offers the images only to show what that brand of sweatshirt looks like, so jurors can compare it with surveillance video of a burglar.

How should the court rule on authentication?
o: Exclude the images, because internet evidence requires testimony from the website's operator.
Admit the images to prove that the defendant bought the sweatshirt from those websites.
Exclude the images, because a social-networking page cannot be attributed to a person without proof he created it.
Admit the images only if they are self-authenticating under Rule 902(6) as periodicals.
Admit them, because what the proponent claims the exhibit is sets how much authentication is needed.
e: Rule: Rule 901 asks whether the item is what the proponent claims, and "the type and quantum of evidence required is related to the purpose for which the evidence is offered" (Oreckinto, quoting Vayner).
oe: Oreckinto held that internet evidence needs no heightened standard.
That would be a different and larger claim, requiring more authentication.
That was Vayner's holding about attributing a page to a defendant. Oreckinto distinguished it, because no one claimed the defendant created the images.
The images were not newspapers or periodicals, and Rule 901 suffices for the limited claim.
Correct. Offered only as a depiction of a commercially available product (like a generic image of a Coca-Cola can), the images needed no testimony from the manufacturer or websites.
topic: Authentication & best evidence — FRE 901 · United States v. Oreckinto

q:
A plaintiff sues in federal court, asserting a federal civil-rights claim and a related state-law tort claim. The defendant seeks a communication protected by a privilege that the state recognizes but federal common law does not. In a separate federal diversity case raising only state-law claims, the same issue arises.

Which statement is correct under Rule 501?
o: Federal common law governs privilege in both cases, because both are in federal court.
State privilege law governs in both cases, because privilege is substantive.
The Federal Rules' Proposed Rules 501–513 govern, because Congress adopted them as federal common law.
State law governs privilege on the state-law claims in both cases; federal law governs the federal claim.
The court must balance the need for the evidence against the privilege in each case.
e: Rule: The common law, as interpreted by United States courts in the light of reason and experience, governs privilege unless the Constitution, a statute, or Supreme Court rules provide otherwise; but in a civil case, state law governs privilege regarding a claim or defense for which state law supplies the rule of decision (FRE 501).
oe: Rule 501's second sentence: in a civil case, state law governs privilege regarding a claim or defense for which state law supplies the rule of decision.
Federal common law governs privilege in criminal cases and on federal claims.
Congress replaced the proposed rules with Rule 501. They remain respected statements of the common law but are not law.

Correct. Rule 501 assigns privilege law claim by claim. Where federal and state claims are joined and the evidence bears on both, the courts must sort out which law governs, the problem the Senate Report predicted.
Rule 501 does not call for ad hoc balancing; Jaffee rejected it for the privileges it recognizes.
topic: Privileges & lawyer-client — FRE 501

q: Which statement about Jaffee v. Redmond is correct?
o: Jaffee recognized a qualified privilege that yields whenever the opposing party's need for the evidence outweighs the patient's privacy interest.
It recognized a privilege for licensed psychotherapists, including clinical social workers, without balancing.
Jaffee recognized a general federal physician-patient privilege.
Jaffee held that a federal court must apply whatever privilege the forum state recognizes in a federal civil-rights case.
Jaffee held that the privilege covers only psychiatrists and psychologists, as Proposed Rule 504 provided.
e: Rule: Confidential communications between a licensed psychotherapist and a patient in the course of diagnosis or treatment are privileged under Rule 501, including communications with licensed clinical social workers, without case-by-case balancing (Jaffee).
oe: Jaffee rejected balancing: "An uncertain privilege ... is little better than no privilege at all."
Correct. Reason: effective therapy depends on confidence, mental health is a public good, and little evidence is lost. Experience: all 50 states and D.C. recognize such a privilege.
There is no federal physician-patient privilege; Jaffee concerned psychotherapists.
Jaffee created a federal common-law privilege under 501. State consensus was evidence of "experience," not binding law; Scalia's dissent called it "inverse pre-emption."
The Court extended it to licensed clinical social workers, though Proposed 504 did not cover them.
topic: Privileges & lawyer-client — Jaffee v. Redmond

q: Which communication is protected by the lawyer-client privilege?
o: A client's answer, on deposition, to the question "Did you sign the contract?", because he discussed the signing with his lawyer.
A prospective client's confidential consultation with a lawyer who then declines the case.
A man's statements to a lawyer friend after the lawyer made clear he would not represent him, during a visit as a friend.
A client's statement to her lawyer, made in a crowded elevator at normal volume, intended for the lawyer's ears alone.
A client's request that her lawyer deliver a stolen item to the police, with instructions to tell them who returned it.
e: Rule: The privilege protects confidential communications between client and lawyer made to facilitate professional legal services. Only the client holds and may waive it, and it protects communications, not the underlying facts.
oe: The privilege protects communications, not underlying facts. The client must answer what he did; he may refuse to say what he told his lawyer.
Correct. Prospective clients are covered even if the lawyer turns down the case; otherwise no one could safely consult a lawyer for the first time.
Gionis held such statements not privileged: the client must consult the lawyer in a professional capacity, and statements after a clear refusal to act are not protected.
Precautions bear on reasonableness. Speaking at normal volume among strangers undercuts the claim that the communication was confidential.
Arranging a return that is meant to be disclosed is not legal advice, and the client intended disclosure (Problem 12.5).
topic: Privileges & lawyer-client — lawyer-client privilege · People v. Gionis

q:
A government agency inadvertently produced a privileged email in a 104-page document production. Five months later, it sent a letter demanding its return. The other side never responded, and the agency did nothing more for three years, until the email appeared on the opponent's exhibit list.

Under Rule 502(b) and Williams, is the privilege waived?
o: No, because any inadvertent disclosure is protected under Rule 502(b).
No, because a single clawback letter under Rule 26(b)(5)(B) fully satisfies Rule 502(b).
Yes, because any disclosure of a privileged document waives the privilege as to all communications on the same subject.
No, because the opposing party had an ethical duty to return the email without reading it.
Yes, because the holder failed to show reasonable steps either to prevent or to rectify the disclosure.
e: Rule: A disclosure in a federal proceeding does not waive the privilege if it was inadvertent, the holder took reasonable steps to prevent it, and the holder promptly took reasonable steps to rectify the error (FRE 502(b)).
oe: Inadvertence is only one of three elements. The holder must also show reasonable steps to prevent disclosure and prompt, reasonable steps to rectify.
Williams held that one letter followed by years of silence was not prompt, reasonable rectification: the privilege "must be jealously guarded by the holder."
Under 502(a), subject-matter waiver requires an intentional waiver, the same subject matter, and fairness. An inadvertent disclosure does not trigger it.
Model Rule 4.4(b) requires only notice to the sender; whether privilege is waived is a question of law under 502(b).
Correct. Unsworn assertions that a paralegal reviewed the documents said nothing about the method, and the small paper production undercut any claim of burden.
topic: Privileges & lawyer-client — FRE 502(b) · Williams v. District of Columbia

q: A grand jury subpoenas a lawyer to name the client who paid her fee. Which situation is most likely to support a privilege claim?
o: The client paid the fee in cash and the government suspects the cash was proceeds of a crime.
The client hired the lawyer for routine traffic matters and paid with a counterfeit bill.
Naming the client would itself reveal a confidential communication.
The client asked the lawyer to keep his identity secret for business reasons.
The lawyer's ethical duty of confidentiality covers the client's identity.
e: Rule: Neither the fee arrangement nor the client's identity is ordinarily privileged, because they are facts that precede the relationship. They are privileged only when revealing them would itself disclose a confidential communication (Osterhoudt; Baird).
oe: Fee arrangements and payment are facts, not confidential communications. Suspicion about the money does not make them privileged.
Alexiou (Problem 12.6) held the identity not privileged: revealing it disclosed no confidence.
Correct. Under the narrow Osterhoudt exception, identity or fee information is privileged only when revealing it would disclose a confidential communication, as in the Baird case.
A request for secrecy does not turn a non-communicative fact into a privileged communication.
The ethical duty of confidentiality is broader than the evidentiary privilege; it does not by itself bar compelled testimony.
topic: Privileges & lawyer-client — lawyer-client privilege · fees and identity

q:
A government lawyer consults private counsel about possible investigations, and the lawyer takes notes. Days later the client dies. A grand jury subpoenas the notes in a criminal investigation, arguing that the privilege should give way after death when the information is important.

What did the Supreme Court hold?
o: The privilege ends at death, because the client no longer has any interest in confidentiality.
The privilege survives death in civil cases but may be overcome in criminal cases by a showing of need.
The privilege survives death, with no balancing exception in criminal cases.
The privilege does not apply to government lawyers consulting private counsel.
The testamentary exception shows that the privilege ends at death for all purposes.
e: Rule: The lawyer-client privilege survives the client's death, and federal courts do not apply case-by-case balancing to overcome it in criminal cases (Swidler & Berlin).
oe: The Court found that clients care about reputation, civil liability, and harm to family after death.
The Court refused to apply the privilege differently in criminal and civil cases.
Correct. Balancing would add the uncertainty Jaffee rejected, and the loss of evidence is "more apparent than real" because clients might not otherwise confide.
Foster consulted private counsel personally, and the Court applied the ordinary privilege.
The testamentary exception carries out the client's wishes; it is not evidence that the privilege ends.
topic: Privileges & lawyer-client — Swidler & Berlin v. United States

q:
The government claims that communications between a client and his lawyers fall within the crime-fraud exception, and asks the court to listen to the recorded conversations in camera. It supports the request with partial transcripts it lawfully obtained from a confidential source.

Which statement reflects Zolin?
o: It may review in camera on a factual basis supporting a reasonable good-faith belief that review may reveal crime-fraud.
The court may not review the communications in camera, because Rule 104(a) binds the court to the rules on privilege.
The court may review the communications in camera only if the government first establishes the exception with independent evidence.
The crime-fraud exception applies to communications about past crimes as well as future ones.
In camera review destroys the privilege, so the court must decide the issue from the government's evidence alone.
e: Rule: Communications made to obtain advice for committing a future crime or fraud are not privileged. Before reviewing allegedly privileged material in camera, the judge should require a factual basis adequate to support a reasonable good-faith belief that review may reveal evidence establishing the exception (Zolin).
oe: Correct. That is Zolin's threshold for in camera review; whether to review is then discretionary, based on the volume of material and the likelihood of success.
Zolin held that 104(a)'s privilege clause does not forbid in camera review to decide whether the crime-fraud exception applies.
The Ninth Circuit required independent evidence, and the Supreme Court vacated. The threshold for review is lower than the showing needed to defeat the privilege.
The exception reaches advice sought for future wrongdoing; communications about past crimes remain fully protected.
Zolin held that in camera review does not destroy the privilege.
topic: Privileges & lawyer-client — crime-fraud exception · United States v. Zolin

q:
A woman arrested with heroin agrees to testify against her husband in exchange for leniency. The husband objects to her testimony.

Under Trammel, who controls the spousal testimonial privilege in federal court?
o: The witness-spouse alone: she may refuse to testify, and he cannot stop her.
The defendant-spouse, who may bar his spouse from testifying against him.
Both spouses, so either may prevent the adverse testimony.
Neither, because the privilege applies only in civil cases.
The court, which balances the need for the testimony against the harm to the marriage.
e: Rule: The witness-spouse alone holds the privilege to refuse to testify adversely against the defendant-spouse; the witness may be neither compelled to testify nor foreclosed from testifying (Trammel).
oe: Correct. When one spouse is willing to testify, there is probably little marital harmony left for the privilege to preserve.
That was the rule of Hawkins v. United States, which Trammel modified.
Trammel gave the privilege to the witness-spouse alone.
The federal testimonial privilege applies only in criminal cases (including grand juries).
Trammel created no balancing test.
topic: Familial privileges — spousal testimonial privilege · Trammel v. United States

q:
A husband is prosecuted for fraud. His wife is willing to testify against him about (1) seeing him shred documents, (2) his statement to her alone at home, "I've been cooking the books," and (3) his statement at a dinner party in front of guests that he would "make the numbers work."

What may she testify to over the husband's objection in federal court?
o: The shredding and the dinner-party remark, but not the private statement, a protected confidence.
None of it, because the husband holds the spousal testimonial privilege.
All of it, because she has waived the spousal testimonial privilege.
Only the private statement, because the testimonial privilege covers acts observed and statements before others.
All of it, unless the couple has since divorced.
e: Rule: The marital confidences privilege covers communications made in confidence during a valid marriage; either spouse may refuse to disclose them and prevent the other from disclosing them. It survives divorce and applies in civil and criminal cases.
oe: Correct. Observations of conduct are not communications, and statements before third parties are not confidential. The private statement is a confidential communication during the marriage, which either spouse may refuse to disclose and prevent the other from disclosing.
Under Trammel, the witness-spouse holds the testimonial privilege, and she is willing.
Her waiver of the testimonial privilege does not waive the husband's marital confidences privilege.
Backwards. The testimonial privilege, which is hers to waive, would cover acts and public statements; the confidences privilege covers the private statement.
Divorce would end the testimonial privilege, but the confidences privilege survives divorce.
topic: Familial privileges — spousal testimonial privilege · marital confidences privilege

q:
A man charged with perjury for denying he was extorted out of his business moves to suppress his conversations with his then-wife about the threats. The government argues that the conversations fall within a crime-fraud exception, that financial matters are not privileged, and that he waived the privilege by telling a creditor he had been forced out.

How did the First Circuit rule in Rakes?
o: The privilege did not apply, because the couple later divorced.
The privilege did not apply, because communications about financial matters are not marital confidences.
The privilege applied only because the couple's infant children were not present.
The privilege was waived, because disclosing the underlying facts to anyone waives the privilege for related communications.
It applied: the exception needs the holder's complicity, and telling a creditor the facts was no waiver.
e: Rule: The marital confidences privilege covers confidential communications during the marriage. Any crime-fraud or joint-crime exception requires wrongful complicity by the privilege holder, and disclosing the underlying facts does not waive the privilege for the communications (Rakes).
oe: The confidences privilege survives divorce if the communications were made during the marriage.
The court found no general exception for financial matters, though money talk may sometimes not be intended as confidential.
The children's presence did not matter; the court held the conversations confidential.
Disclosing facts is not disclosing the communication, so there was no waiver.
Correct. Calling extortion victims participants was "Orwellian," and the privilege covers communications, not the underlying facts.
topic: Familial privileges — marital confidences privilege · United States v. Rakes

q: Which communication between spouses is most likely protected by the marital confidences privilege?
o: A note one spouse left the other in their shared home, whose contents nothing suggests anyone else read, written while the couple was married.
An email to his wife that a husband sent from his employer's computer system, which displayed a log-on banner warning that users have no expectation of privacy.
A statement a wife made to her husband before they married, which the husband now wants to disclose.
A statement a husband made to his wife in front of their adult houseguest.
A conversation in which the spouses planned a fraud they later carried out together.
e: Rule: The marital confidences privilege requires a communication, made in confidence (presumed, but defeated by third parties or a lack of any reasonable expectation of privacy), during a valid marriage.
oe: Correct. Marital communications are presumed confidential, and a note between spouses at home can qualify (Montgomery, Problem 13.3).
Etkin (Problem 13.2) held such an email not privileged: no reasonable expectation of confidentiality, even if he never read the banner.
The confidences privilege covers only communications made during a valid marriage.
The presence of third parties defeats confidentiality.
Almost all circuits deny the privilege for communications about joint ongoing or future crimes.
topic: Familial privileges — marital confidences privilege · confidentiality

q:
A federal grand jury subpoenas a father to testify about conversations with his adult son, the target of the investigation. The father argues that compelled testimony would destroy their close relationship.

What is the likely result in federal court?
o: The father may refuse, because federal courts recognize a parent-child privilege by analogy to the spousal privilege.
The father may refuse, because Jaffee requires recognizing privileges that protect important relationships.
The father must testify only if the son is an adult; communications with minor children are privileged.
The father may refuse, because Rule 501 incorporates the privileges of the state where the grand jury sits.
He must testify, because federal courts recognize no parent-child privilege.
e: Rule: Federal courts do not recognize a parent-child privilege. Under Rule 501's "reason and experience" standard, it lacks a consensus among the states and did not exist at common law.
oe: Almost every court rejects a parent-child privilege; no federal court of appeals had recognized one.
Jaffee's test includes "experience": a consensus among the states. The parent-child privilege lacks it.

The Third Circuit rejected the privilege in both consolidated appeals, including one involving a minor daughter; the partial dissent would have recognized a limited privilege for a child's request for parental advice.
Federal common law governs privilege in criminal proceedings.
Correct. In re Grand Jury Proceedings (3d Cir. 1997) found only four states protecting such communications and held that any privilege should come from Congress.
topic: Familial privileges — parent-child privilege · Jaffee v. Redmond
